hops.title: Stare at the ceiling for a minute
hops.text: Gaze at a spot high on the wall for a full minute without tipping your head back. Your lids stay up because the levator muscle keeps firing. That steadiness depends partly on receptor packing: a healthy junction holds roughly 10,000 acetylcholine receptors per square micrometer at the crests of the folds under the nerve. Rodent junctions have a safety factor of about four. Human terminals typically release 20 to 30 quanta per impulse, so ours is about two during low-frequency stimulation. In the Simpson test for myasthenia gravis, one to two minutes of looking as high as possible can bring out or worsen a drooping eyelid.

image.caption: During upward gaze, the levator muscle holds your eyelids up, and densely packed receptors help keep its junctions firing.

hops.afterHeading: How the nerve's signal was found
hops.title: A krait toxin from a postwar Taipei lab
hops.text: In 1963, in a poorly funded, underequipped pharmacology lab at National Taiwan University, during the lean and isolated years after the Second World War, Chuan-Chiung Chang and Chen-Yuan Lee pulled a small protein out of the venom of Taiwan's banded krait, Bungarus multicinctus. They named it alpha-bungarotoxin. It binds the muscle acetylcholine receptor specifically and does not let go, which made it an ideal tag. In 1970 Changeux, Kasai and Lee used it to show that a protein isolated from electric tissue behaved as the cholinergic receptor. The toxin later helped researchers raise antibodies against that receptor and, eventually, build an experimental autoimmune model of myasthenia gravis.

sources.citation: Chu NS. Contribution of a snake venom toxin to myasthenia gravis: the discovery of alpha-bungarotoxin in Taiwan. J Hist Neurosci. 2005;14(2):138-148.
Changeux JP, Kasai M, Lee CY. Use of a snake venom toxin to characterize the cholinergic receptor protein. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 1970;67(3):1241-1247.

image.caption: A krait toxin purified in a cash-strapped Taipei lab became the tag that pinned down the muscle's acetylcholine receptor.

hops.afterHeading: NMJ vs. central synapses, and a junction that fails
hops.title: Why dogs with myasthenia gravis eat upright
hops.text: Swallowing works differently in a dog. The lower third of the human esophagus is smooth muscle, but the muscle of a dog's esophageal body is skeletal, run by acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions. In a 2025 study of 167 dogs with myasthenia gravis, 66 of 77 assessed in the study's 83-dog antibody-positive generalized subgroup had megaesophagus (a widened esophagus) or impaired esophageal movement. Many of these dogs are fed sitting upright in a Bailey chair so gravity can help. Even upright, transit varies. In an imaging study of twelve dogs with megaesophagus from several causes, two of them myasthenic, canned-food meatballs cleared completely within thirty minutes in only three.
